For a one-electron (hydrogen-like) system the orbit radius is \(r_n = \dfrac{n^2 h^2 \varepsilon_0}{\pi m_e Z e^2} = \dfrac{n^2}{Z}a_0\), so for the first orbit \((n = 1)\) the radius varies as \(1/Z\).

Hydrogen, the deuteron (deuterium) and tritium are all isotopes of hydrogen and so all have \(Z = 1\); only singly ionized helium \((\text{He}^{+})\) has \(Z = 2\).

\(r_1(\text{He}^{+}) = a_0/2\), against \(r_1 \approx a_0\) for the other three. The heavier nuclei of the deuteron and tritium do shrink the radius, but only through the reduced mass and only by about 0.03% and 0.05% — far too little to compete with halving.

Hence the radius of the first orbit is smallest for singly ionized helium.

The radius of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) Bohr orbit is proportional to \(n^2\): \(r_n = a_0 n^2\).

\(\dfrac{r_8}{r_4} = \dfrac{8^2}{4^2} = \dfrac{64}{16} = 4\)

So the 4th orbit is smaller than the 8th by a factor of 4.

By Rydberg's formula \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2} - \dfrac{1}{m^2}\right)\), so the longest wavelength belongs to the transition with the SMALLEST value of the bracket, i.e. the smallest energy difference.

For the four transitions:

\(n = 2 \to 1:\ \dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2} = 0.7500\)

\(n = 5 \to 4:\ \dfrac{1}{4^2} - \dfrac{1}{5^2} = 0.02250\)

\(n = 7 \to 6:\ \dfrac{1}{6^2} - \dfrac{1}{7^2} = 0.007370\)

\(n = 8 \to 7:\ \dfrac{1}{7^2} - \dfrac{1}{8^2} = 0.004783\)

The smallest bracket is for \(n = 8\) to \(n = 7\), so that transition yields the longest wavelength.

The nuclear radius is \(R = R_0 A^{1/3}\), so it grows with the mass number \(A\). The volume \(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A\) is directly proportional to \(A\), and the mass is approximately \(A\) times the mass of one nucleon, so it too grows with \(A\).

The density, however, is

\(\rho = \dfrac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}\)

in which \(A\) cancels. Numerically it is about \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}\) for every nucleus.

So density is the property that does not depend on the mass number.

In each half-life the number of undecayed parent nuclei falls to half its value, so after \(n\) half-lives the number left is \(N/2^{n}\).

After one half-life: \(N/2\). After a second half-life: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{N}{2} = \dfrac{N}{4}\).

So at the end of two half-lives the number of nuclei is \(N/4\).
